Isn't this expected? It is upgrading to a different protocol. The HTTP parser is freed after the `'upgrade'` event.

> Isn't this expected?

Not to me. Node can tell if there is a body just like any normal HTTP request and so it should be able to parse that. This is very useful if you want to pass information to the server before switching protocols and without resorting to spamming the querystring or headers.

FWIW, it worked like this since forever, and I think it makes sense. You can't tell beforehand if the body need to be used as data for the upgraded protocol. For example, even though the WebSocket protocol spec specifies that no data should be exchanged until the opening handshake is complete, a lot of implementations use the body of the handshake request as WebSocket data. I think this is also why the callback of the `'upgrade'` events takes the `head` parameter.

> You can't tell beforehand if the body need to be used as data for the upgraded protocol.

Why would a client bother sending a body (in the HTTP sense indicated via `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding: chunked`) if they could just send the same data as part of the upgraded protocol (whether it's before or after the server sends the 101 response)?

> For example, even though the WebSocket protocol spec specifies that no data should be exchanged until the opening handshake is complete, a lot of implementations use the body of the handshake request as WebSocket data.

The difference is that [WebSocket requests *must* be GET requests](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455#page-17), which means they can never have a body, so there is no problem there.

It's only a problem for other/custom upgraded protocols that allow non-GET upgrade requests.

> Why would a client bother sending a body (in the HTTP sense indicated via Content-Length or Transfer-Encoding: chunked) if they could just send the same data as part of the upgraded protocol (whether it's before or after the server sends the 101 response)?

How and when do you decide to which protocol the incoming data belongs to?

> The difference is that [WebSocket requests must be GET requests](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455#page-17), which means they can never have a body, so there is no problem there.

There are misbehaving clients that actually send data in the body of the initial GET request.

> How and when do you decide to which protocol the incoming data belongs to?

I see two scenarios:

1. A client has indicated their HTTP request includes a body. Any upgraded protocol data would come immediately after the end of the body.

2. A client has *not* indicated their HTTP request includes a body. Any upgraded protocol data would come immediately after the end of the client HTTP headers.

> There are misbehaving clients that actually send data in the body of the initial GET request.

Perhaps there are, but how common is that? I would wager that browsers make up the bulk majority of WebSocket requests, which do not misbehave (especially in 2025).

Additionally, there should be a distinction between misbehaving WebSocket clients sending handshake data immediately after the HTTP headers and those who are indicating an HTTP body in their request (by setting the appropriate HTTP headers). The former does not matter because they never indicated there was a body to be parsed and the latter is a bit of a moot case because the client is just extra broken at that point (and if node really wanted to care about that kind of case, you could just check for that specific scenario -- GET + "Upgrade: Websocket" + HTTP body).
I never investigated, but is the current behavior Node.js specific?  Is there anything about this in HTTP spec? How are other runtimes / languages handling this?

> Is there anything about this in HTTP spec?

The [current RFC says this about upgrade requests:](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-7.8) (emphasis mine)

  > A client cannot begin using an upgraded protocol on the connection until it has completely sent <ins>the request message</ins> (i.e., the client can't change the protocol it is sending in the middle of a message).

[Earlier in the same RFC](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#name-message-abstraction) it describes the definition of a "message", which includes everything from the first line containing (in the case of a request) the method and path to the optional HTTP trailers.

This seems to align with my expectation that the server should be processing any HTTP request body as normal and anything after that is processed as the upgraded protocol (if the server sends a 101).

Pretty sure @mscdex is right and that properly included bodies (e.g. `content-length: N` + body) should be considered part of the request, not the upgrade stream. Unfortunately llhttp doesn't support that at all, and always assumes there's no body if you upgrade (see the return values for `on_headers_complete` in https://github.com/nodejs/llhttp).

I'll ping @nodejs/workers, can I ask why aren't v8 options supported for a worker thread? Is there a feasible way to support them? Or at least a handful of them? This `--disallow-code-generation-from-strings` seems a quite interesting security feature -as OP mentioned-.

Refs: https://nodejs.org/docs/latest/api/worker_threads.html#new-workerfilename-options

> can I ask why aren't v8 options supported for a worker thread?

Most V8 flags are per process flags. Changing it for one worker thread will also change the flag value for other threads.

This per-process storage applies to `--disallow-code-generation-from-strings` as well. It is the default value for new context's code generation setting, for _all_ threads.

In addition, `--disallow-code-generation-from-strings` is not a security flag. It is implemented in V8 and only disallows `eval` and `new Function`: https://github.com/nodejs/node/pull/58328

> This means, as far as I can tell, all objects constructed through napi will end up in the slow dictionary mode

Dictionary mode happens when an object has too many properties. In that respect `ObjectTemplate` vs. adding properties one by one doesn't matter.

Instantiating an `ObjectTemplate` is marginally faster because you're not going through the JS engine's "add property to object" code path repeatedly but it won't be noticeable unless you create millions of objects or your objects have many properties.

As a practical concern: support for JS engines other than V8 is a design goal of n-api and I don't think other engines have a concept that maps cleanly to `ObjecTemplate`.  Spidermonkey's `JSClass` for example isn't a 1-to-1 fit.

So far it seems that Node-API or V8 API cannot create JS objects as fast as the JS parser does from object literals. It makes sense: the parser has the full information upfront and can optimize the creation unlike anything we can do through the API. Adding a special V8 API as for JSON object might address this issue. But frankly, it all feels a bit wrong: on one side we have C++ or Rust that can be extremely efficient with handling large amount of data, and on the other side we have JavaScript that was never meant to be that efficient, and still when we use C++ we lose. The reason we lose is because we make C++ to play by JavaScript rules. Since the interop has an overhead, we theoretically cannot achieve the same perf as in JavaScript. The only way to win is to avoid playing by JavaScript rules. It means avoiding creation a lot of small objects from C++ and instead explore other techniques.

My understanding is that these small objects are needed to represent some UI scene graphs. Games written in C++ often avoid creation of many small objects and instead use arrays for better cache locality. Thus, the proposal is to rethink the JS code that works with the native APIs in a way that it keeps data mostly in big arrays and is not "chatty".
-  The data that is kept in native arrays can be either completely native or be exposed to JS code through TypedArrays or Buffers. 
- The API must not be "chatty": any call to the native code must result in some "juicy action" - a non-trivial work done by native code to process the data structures. This way any interop overhead will be negligible comparing with the useful work.

I don't know how it works in V8, but in JSC there is an explicit JSC::Structure class which holds the properties defined for an object and the structure can be reused for multiple objects. 

To create new objects with the same properties quickly in JSC, we can:
1) define the structure once with all the properties added
2) put the properties onto the objects in the same order the properties were defined

It has a special fast path when there are under 64 properties and then a fast but not as fast path for objects with more than 63 properties  

The particular types of the properties in the JSC::Structure don't matter much. It only needs to know how many, what are the property names, and what are the attributes 

It's fastest to persistently hold on to a Structure if it's going to be reused, but then it needs to be visited by the garbage collector and that's tricky because who owns it? In bun's case, we use this optimization in a couple places and we lazily mark it as owned by the global object which means once created, it's never freed. This is okay because we are selective of when we do this optimization 

I recommend against going the approach of using getter/setters because it will make the runtime performance of using the objects worse due to lack of inlining.

My current thinking is that we must add three different API sets to the Node-API:
- Fast object creation.
- Fast array creation.
- Create internalized strings.

The fast object creation can be achieved by
- Providing existing object that can be used as a template. Hopefully we can reuse its hidden class.
- Providing the full set of property name-value pairs when no template is given. Otherwise, it will provide only the delta for the template.

The API will essentially combine JavaScript [Object initializer](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Operators/Object_initializer), [Object.assign()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/assign), and [Object.fromEntries()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/Object/fromEntries) behavior.

This API will have one significant drawback - it will not support property descriptors and focus only on the writable, enumerable, and configurable value properties. Is it a big disadvantage? Should we use the property descriptors as @kjvalencik proposed above?

The fast array creation should mimic the JavaScript [Array literals](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Guide/Grammar_and_types#array_literals). There can be three overloads: for Integers, Doubles, and general napi_value. The hope is that knowing the size and type of values we can improve the initial array creation speed.

The string internalizing can give advantage for the V8 and other JS engines. The JS engines that do not support it can just return a regular string.

Thus, the full list of new APIs may look like:
``` C++
napi_status node_api_create_object_from_entries(
  napi_env env,
  napi_value object_tempate, // optional object to clone
  napi_value prototype, // either object or null to use when no object_tempate given
  size_t property_count, // number of names and values entries
  napi_value* names,
  napi_value* values,
  napi_value* result);

napi_status node_api_create_array_int32(napi_env env, size_t count, int32_t* values, napi_value* result);
napi_status node_api_create_array_double(napi_env env, size_t count, double* values, napi_value* result);
napi_status node_api_create_array_from_values(napi_env env, size_t count, napi_value* values, napi_value* result);

napi_status node_api_create_property_key_utf8(napi_env env, const char* str, size_t length, napi_value* result);
napi_status node_api_create_property_key_utf16(napi_env env, const char16_t* str, size_t length, napi_value* result);
napi_status node_api_create_property_key(napi_env env, napi_value str_or_sym, napi_value* result);

```

Looks good to me! 

> Should we use the property descriptors

I think this is a much more rare use case, so it's ok if it's done through a different API that isn't as optimized. This would be similar to creating an object literal in JS vs `Object.create`.

> Should we use the property descriptors

I wasn't proposing it, just benchmarking. I don't think this is necessary.

> There can be three overloads: for Integers, Doubles, and general napi_value

I think only `napi_value` is necessary. Numeric values are already handled well by typed arrays which can usually be created with a simple `memcpy`.

Hey, it took me a long time to start working on research again as I didn't have a good design API in mind around this logging feature. Initially, I tried to create something from scratch, but then I realized that it would be better to rely on a more mature and stable API, like Pino.

So I [created a repository to write a wrapper](https://github.com/H4ad/nodejs-logging-proposal) around `Pino` that exposes three methods:
- `setOptions`: To customize the options of the main pin instance.
- `getLogger`: To get a child instance of the main instance (configured via `setOptions`).
- `buildTransport`: Basically exposes a way to create new transports for pino.

I wrote more details about which properties are exposed and how each method behaves in the repository, so I recommend you take a look at the wrapper implementation, which is quite simple (less than 200 lines).

For me, the main advantage of using `pino` is the solid foundation around the transports that Matteo talks more about [in this video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vETUVN-KEgc).

In terms of extensibility, it is very easy to introduce or let users create new transports using `buildTransport`, currently the main transport is `stdout` but we can expose transports to store the logs in `file`, or send via `http` and many others.

Please have a look at the repository ([link](https://github.com/H4ad/nodejs-logging-proposal)) and tell me what you guys think about this approach, there are a lot of things I don't know yet, like:

- How do we want to include pino in Node, exactly like `undici` or do we want to completely rewrite it?
- What transports do we want to showcase?
- Are these three methods I exposed enough to create a PR to start this experimental feature? Later we can present the other parts/transports and expose them via `node:logging/transports/file`.
- Should we expose the redact or should we just remove that part to avoid security issues?

Also, to advance this proposal, I created a bunch of issues on the [nodejs-logging-proposal](https://github.com/H4ad/nodejs-logging-proposal/issues) repository to try to advance the implementation and have more feedback about each aspect, so feel free to open more issues or add comments to each issue.

This issue came to my attention because of #58897, and I wanted to mention (and repeat a few points from above) a few cautionary things having helped run one of the larger single deployments of `pino` out there these past years.

1. `pino` is for (high concurrency) servers. This is *great* if that is your use case, but it's api and underlying complexity is not well suited to all use cases. There is room for something between `console.log` and `pino` (partly covered above). Core's api should be careful not to lean too heavily into those types of opinions if possible.
2. Buffering logs can be hard to get right even within a server using `pino`. This is one of those things that can be a tricky balance, especially for beginners to understand/debug. By taking on this api surface, Node.js will likely be taking on some responsibility in documenting and teaching this. Before getting to "implement a logging interface" it would be good to spend some cycles on this expanding [this section](https://github.com/pinojs/pino/blob/main/docs/asynchronous.md) of docs.
3. `pino`'s choice to put the "merge"/context object before the message is a regular and constant foot gun even for our mostly experienced user base. Would be great to address that before porting this api into core.
4. Formatting the structured logs for humans is pretty important. I say this because we didn't do a great job of this and for local development our users hate it. Similar to how the tap output from the built in test runner is generally disliked and `spec` is now the default, this will likely be a high priority need for a structured logger.

I probably have other thoughts but didn't really even have proper time to invest in what I have here, so will leave this less than well edited comment as it.

To be clear, I am not blaming Pino. I think it has a few great advantages for the use case it was designed for. I am just saying that it is a footgun for users because it doesn't blow up when they do it wrong, and they often do it wrong. As for compatibility, I think that *was* a valid concern but honestly for this discussion I think a Node.js core api should be a building block *first* and a direct use api *second*. Last week I tried to create a util.log method to address logging
performance issues. @mcollina provided feedback in #60116:

https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/49296.

Following that suggestion, I'd like to contribute to this issue.

### Research Summary

  I looked at:
  - **Go slog**: Handler pattern (TextHandler, JSONHandler), structured
   key-value pairs
  - **Rust tracing**: Spans for execution context, hierarchical logging
  - **Pino**: Async transports, off-thread processing, performance
  optimizations

  ### Observations from Discussion

  Reading through the thread, I see a few key themes:

  1. **Handler pattern is essential** (echoing @jsumners and
  @wesleytodd)
     - Allows different output formats (JSON, text, custom)
     - Solves the CLI vs server use case problem

  2. **Building block approach** (@wesleytodd's point)
     - Core provides structured logging primitives
     - Formatters/handlers can be swapped
     - Avoids pino's argument order footgun

  3. **SonicBoom port in progress** (@jasnell #58897)
     - ThreadStream still needed - I'd be happy to help with this

  ### Proposed Direction (Initial Thoughts)

  Based on the research and discussion:

  ```javascript
  // Simple, building-block API
  const { createLogger, JSONHandler, TextHandler } =
  require('node:log');

  // JSON for servers (default)
  const logger = createLogger({
    handler: new JSONHandler({ level: 'info' })
  });

  logger.info('user login', { userId: 123, ip: '192.168.1.1' });

  // Text for CLI (human-readable)
  const cliLogger = createLogger({
    handler: new TextHandler({ colorize: true })
  });

  // Custom handlers for flexibility
  class MyHandler {
    handle(record) { /* custom logic */ }
  }
```

  Key principles:
  - Handler pattern (Go slog)
  - Object-first for structured logging (avoids pino's footgun)
  - Drop-in compatible via custom handlers
  - Performance via SonicBoom + ThreadStream

  OTEL. Should we consider this as an output target rather than
  reinventing? Or is stdlib logging orthogonal?
  2. ThreadStream: @jasnell mentioned this needs to be ported. I'd be
  happy to take this on if there's consensus on the direction. Any
  design constraints?
  3. API naming: node:log vs node:logger vs node:logging?

  Next Steps

  Happy to:
  - Work on ThreadStream port
  - Create an RFC with detailed API proposal
  - Build a prototype once we have consensus

  Thoughts?

Regarding log levels: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5424 (like winston). This should be an option of the logger constructor.

Just so you know, you are missing child loggers in your proposal.

Regarding object order for logs, how would the following be rendered as JSON?

```js
logger.info('user login', { userId: 123, ip: '192.168.1.1' });
```

The practical reason for having a single object at the front is that it's clear that it will be meshed inside the actual JSON line. You can't do that with variadic forms.

See @wesleytodd [comment](https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/49296#issuecomment-3160310119) above, I think we should be targeting this instead:

```js
logger.info({ msg: 'user login', userId: 123, ip: '192.168.1.1' });
```

OTEL integration should be done via an handler/transport.

I find the behavior of the following logline intuitive based on prior third party logging libraries. 

```js
/** (msg: string, values: Record<string, any>) => void */
logger.info('the user attempt a login', {
  userId: 123,
  ip: '192.168.1.1',
  reqHeaders: req.headers
})
```

It is to format something like `{ msg: 'user login', userId: 123, ip: '192.168.1.1', reqHeaders: { ... }  }` to the output destination.

The benefit of having two arguments is
 - The log message can become a mandatory argument, there's not much value without it.
 - The logline is formatted to always have the message first and the dynamic parameters last, instead of having the log message somewhere as the Nth object field.
 - The documentation can strongly encourage developers to use static log messages ( discourage string templates or dynamic strings ) which is the value proposition of structured logging, to have something to switch on in your log search engine.
 - the API can force `logger.info('user login', {})` to be the smallest logline, which is significantly more useful then `logger.info({})` 

Worst case large log lines are formatted as 

```js
       logger.info('Packagist: done with pollPackages for backfill', {
        offset: i,
        batchCounter,
      })
```

Putting the message last or inline leads formatters to do

```js
      logger.info(
        {
          offset: i,
          batchCounter,
        },
        'Packagist: done with pollPackages for backfill',
      )
```

Having an exactly two argument implementation with both mandatory is ergonomic and intuitive in it's behavior. It may have to build a new object to be stringified to JSON and has more object allocation overhead over a different API, but that could be solved with a lower level API being exposed so user libraries like `pino` can re-use `node:log` without minimal performance penalty.

> * Aligns with existing ecosystem (Pino, Winston, Bunyan all use message-first)

Not so. Pino's first argument is an optional "merging object." We routinely get people asking for `log('msg', { object: { to: { be: 'serialized' } } })` and I have to point them to our `logMethod` hook. Basically, they expect the wacky behavior of `console.log('something', 'anything', 'else', { foo: 'bar' })`. Whereas Pino follows the much more industry standard of a format string based logger approach (which is more efficient).

> Quick question: should `fatal()` exit the process or just log at critical level?

If it's going to exit, the docs should be as clear as https://pkg.go.dev/log#Fatal


> Fatal is equivalent to [Print](https://pkg.go.dev/log#Print) followed by a call to [os.Exit](https://pkg.go.dev/os#Exit)(1).
> ...
> ...
> Exit causes the current program to exit with the given status code. Conventionally, code zero indicates success, non-zero an error. The program terminates immediately; **deferred functions are not run.**

(emphasis mine)

I don't think I like loggers affecting the process, though. I get the idea, but it just feels very wrong.

> I'll switch to RFC5424 levels (trace/debug/info/warn/error/fatal).

I could be wrong, but I think the main thing to follow with that RFC is the numerical ordering for severity levels. Pino has it backward in that the numerical representation has more verbose at a lower value and less verbose at a higher value (https://github.com/pinojs/pino-syslog/blob/883eb0786ee69d7e64588150104ac72dff64bdaf/lib/utils.js#L3-L35). In terms of methods, in my experience the industry generally follows the log4j interface (https://logging.apache.org/log4j/2.x/javadoc/log4j-api/org/apache/logging/log4j/Level.html).

Hello, we spoke with @ovflowd recently and he mentioned a few valid concerns that I would like to share with you as well. 

API Design and Scope Concerns:
Claudio emphasized that this issue could be challenging not from a technical implementation perspective, but in terms of API design, scope, and usability. He particularly highlighted the following points:

Standard Compatibility: Since console.* APIs are standard across all runtimes, adding a Node.js-specific logging solution could be quite disruptive.
Cross-Runtime Compatibility: Risk of creating problems for codebases written for the web that are intended to run on mixed or different runtimes.
Risk of Non-Spec Features: Adding a non-spec feature for a fundamental functionality like logging carries the risk of criticism and backlash.

Recommended Roadmap
Claudio stated that it would be much more logical to first approach platforms like WinterTC to work on a solution that could be standardized across runtimes. This approach could ensure wider acceptance of the proposal and add real value.

> Standard Compatibility: Since console.* APIs are standard across all runtimes, adding a Node.js-specific logging solution could be quite disruptive.

In my opinion, the `console.*` methods are irrelevant. They were invented by a browser at the same time in-browser developer tools were invented. They are being retconned into a standard, but are certainly _not_ standard as-is. Even if they are standardized, or considered as such, they are still not a proper logging solution. In particular, they don't solve the _structured logging_ problem.

> Cross-Runtime Compatibility: Risk of creating problems for codebases written for the web that are intended to run on mixed or different runtimes.

Personally: do not care. Node.js is not a web nor a mixed environment.

> Risk of Non-Spec Features: Adding a non-spec feature for a fundamental functionality like logging carries the risk of criticism and backlash.

My opinion is that this is also irrelevant. I would ship several more opinionated things in core that would get a lot more hate than a standardized logger that no one actually _has_ to use.

> Claudio stated that it would be much more logical to first approach platforms like WinterTC to work on a solution that could be standardized across runtimes. This approach could ensure wider acceptance of the proposal and add real value.

Again, my opinion is: 👎 . This issue is about adding a standardized logger as a core feature of Node.js. What other committees and runtimes want to add is up to them. They shouldn't have any influence on what Node.js wants to add as features for itself and its community.

Structured logging is something I actually intended to do with diagnostics_channel at some point but I just have not got to it yet. Subcscriptions can be used to enable/disable different log levels, and all serialization, flushing, and writing out to whichever target is desired can be offloaded entirely to the subscribers, so it's a good mechanism for providing the public-facing part of a logging API. It also allows multi-tenancy and high performance already, so it's actually a quite suitable core for such a system.

Ultimately, we would want to provide an adapter for Console similar to https://github.com/pinojs/pino-console. That would be valuable to do.

> Claudio stated that it would be much more logical to first approach platforms like WinterTC to work on a solution that could be standardized across runtimes. This approach could ensure wider acceptance of the proposal and add real value.

I'm not interested because historically, spec-driven development has resulted in slower implementations for Node.js. I want a fast logging solution for Node.js, not one that compromises the needs of other runtimes. We could, however, standardize on a subset of public APIs so that users would know what to expect if they want to implement something cross-runtime.

My :2cents:, ultimately we do what's best for Node, but that doesn't mean what's best for Node couldn't be also what's best for others. I don't see harm into knocking WinterTC's door and reach into an agreement of a standard subset of public APIs for our logger.

That doesn't mean our implementation and public APIs should be limited by whatever we agree on WinterTC, for all I care our logger could superseed/extend that set of APIs. My goal here is to ensure that at the very least there was dialogue. Logging is something quite universal, and why not making something standardized (?)

Now, regarding the logger implementation, that should absolutely be on Node's domain, such as `node:log` and not a global/standardized class/implementation.

That doesn't mean that whatever we end up implementing ie:

```tsx
import { createLogger } from 'node:log';

const logger = createLogger({ transport: WhateverStreamInterface ) // just example code
```

My point is that createLogger would implement an interface ie: `NodeLogger extends WhateverStandardInterface`

I also don't like the idea of "do not care about others, ship whatever we want", of course Node is in a leading position where we drive the usage. But doesn't mean we gotta silo ourselves and go with whatever we want in disregard of what others would like to see on a standard space. I admit that at the end of the day we serve our community and our users and should solve for what's best for Node, that doesn't mean we should completely ignore the outer community.

@ovflowd, my key point is that `WhateverStreamInterface` would involve a WHATWG-standardized `WritableStream`, resulting in a solution _slower_ than pino. A key success criterion should be to create a library as fast as pino if not faster. This is _not possible_ with the implementation of WHATWG streams that Node.js has.

What I'm saying is that we should instead focus on the public API:

```js
import { createLogger } from 'node:logger'

const logger: StandardLogger = createLogger()

logger.info({ msg: 'hello' })
```

Focus on the usage API and not the transport mechanism, and keep those that are not portable or runtime specific.
The stream interface was just an example. We can implement transports whatever and however we want (if we even want to do that)

I'm with you. I haven't responded to this direct question because I haven't been able to come to a conclusion on what I'd like to see. I don't like `info({ merging: 'object' }, 'message')`, and I prefer `info('message', { merging: 'object' })`. But I can see the argument for `info({ msg: 'message', other: 'fields' })` being easier to implement and maintain.

While I appreciate Go's `slog` package, I am not a fan of the `info('message', 'key1', 'value1', ...)` approach.

One thing I haven't seen discussed -- and totally fine if this is not included in the design -- is how and whether `Error` objects would be serialized.  Just doing `JSON.stringify()` is unsatisfying:

```
> JSON.stringify(new Error('boom'))
'{}'
```

So having some way for the user to relatively-easily have a nice serialization of error objects would be nice.

This *can* impact the interface. For example pino and bunyan have a special case for the first argument being an error instance: `logger.info(new Error('boom'))`.   They also special case the "err" field name to do `Error`-serialization -- at least by default.

On the other hand, adding any sort of special handing of arguments or fields adds some complexity.

> I don't like `info({ merging: 'object' }, 'message')`, and I prefer `info('message', { merging: 'object' })`. 

I thought Raynos did a good job [arguing for message first `info('hi', {foo:'bar'})` over merging-object first](https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/49296#issuecomment-3372855491) above.  The reason "merging-object first" exists is because I wanted to support varargs-style in Bunyan at the time, to be closer to `console.log()`. Since then, (a) JS grew string templates for those that really want a varying message and (b) personally I've come to prefer a static string key for the msg (as Raynos was arguing for).

Either of `info({ merging: 'object' }, 'message')` or `info('message', { merging: 'object' })` will need to then merge the object and the message together somehow anyway, so it makes the _most_ sense to me to just do `info({ message: 'message', other: ... })`.

We can safely support two arguments, ideally with the string first.

We would need to have an internal data structure anyway:

1. time (maybe this can actually be avoided, which would be best)
2. level
3. message
4. merging

So that you know, I recommend avoiding merging at the first step and delegating this to transports / formatters. We would lose some perf compared to pino, but it would allow for a clearer standardization.

I have been thinking about this and I'm unsure about the viability when thinking about destinations. There are a few people that want to stream to different destinations based upon log level, and this would certainly make that possible, but the typical case is streaming everything to a single destination with interleaved levels. Which leads to ordering: I'm not clear if the proposed approach would be able to guarantee ordering of logs. People _really_ don't like it when Log Line B is written before Log Line A.

Yes it would allow supporting the ordering of logs.

The question on using diagnostic_channels for this is how can we support a destination only receiving logs from a given logger.

This might not be a use case we want to support. If we don't, having a `createLogger()` might be redundant.

If we give each logger a unique name, we could map to channels like `log:info:grandparent:parent:child` or something like that. Easy enough to support listening to specific loggers if that's a thing we want. We can also have a discovery channel like `log:new` to be notified any time a new logger is constructed to decide if the channel is worth subscribing to.

The problem is `lib/typescript.js` being 200k lines of code. My hunch was that adding a `type: "commonjs"` to typescript `package.json` would have fixed it, but it didn't help.
I believe renaming it to `.cjs` would fix it; no "type" required.

`cjs-module-lexer` isn't determining whether the file is CommonJS or ESM, it's trying to determine the named exports so that you can write code like `import { compile } from 'typescript'`. It needs to do that no matter how explicit the filename or `package.json` is. The performance impact is magnified here because `lib/typescript.js` is gigantic.

Perhaps there's some optimization that can be done when we know that the importing file is asking for just the default export—`import typescript from 'typescript'`—as is the case here; but I feel like that's probably difficult if not impossible to know at the point we're loading the file, and since the same file could have multiple importers and to do this optimization we'd have to be sure that none of the importers are requesting named exports. And if we did made this change, then we'd create a performance incentive to prefer importing a module's default export which I think is generally considered an antipattern.

In this particular case, perhaps `createRequire` could be used:

```js
import { createRequire } from 'node:module'
const require = createRequre(import.meta.url)
const typescript = require('typescript')
```

And I would expect this to have almost equivalent performance to the CommonJS example. So maybe this is what users can do for the edge case of loading a huge CommonJS file into an ESM context. But I don't think there's much more we can do, as we don't want to remove the ability for users to import named exports from CommonJS and that's a feature that's worth the usually-negligible performance impact.

Did we check what code is hot in the lexer during loading? I could imagine we could optimize something or find some other short cuts that would improve the loading time.

I also like the idea of skipping the exports, if they are not needed. We could likely have a state that would just mark something as it needs exports the first time it's encountered and the lexer is run in that moment instead of before.

>  since the same file could have multiple importers and to do this optimization we'd have to be sure that none of the importers are requesting named exports.

I think this would be a deal breaker, because dynamic import() is a thing 😬

If the overhead indeed comes from the lexer, optimising it might help but I suspect that when processing huge files the overhead is still going to be significant. The most viable option might be to just use createRequire() to skip the lexing entirely.

Another potential solution would be something like https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/50981 - inventing a directive or something that does not require scanning the whole file to obtain the keys of the named exports. But that still counts on the CommonJS module to use it.

I guess there are no easy win here, and we would need to ship something like #5091.

@GeoffreyBooth can you confirm that converting to ESM would actually fix the problem?

I know we like to fast-track those `npm` PRs, but the risk of breaking the ecosystem is real. (Something we can do in addition or instead is run CITGM nightly, but we may already do that, and the issue with nightly runs is that people tend to not look at them. I used to watch the daily CI run and I'm pretty sure I'm the only one. I stopped and it's been failing for months at this point.)

> It does seem like this issue should have been caught by CITGM, which I believe the releasers run, but maybe only when they expect a breaking change and therefore not on LTS releases

CITGM should be run on every release, and it usually is as it is part of the documented release process. We only rarely do not run it - typically only in the case of urgent security or bug fixes where we know the CITGM run results would be unlikely to alter our decision to include a patch.

> but it does appear that [UglifyJS is skipped as flaky in at least some situations](https://github.com/nodejs/citgm/blob/bc85e2e25eb5613a1d0cf8c7a376aec47aae38da/lib/lookup.json#L524-L530).

With `"skip": ["12", true],` - I believe `true` means that it's skipped on all versions, all platforms, all of the time - so it's not entirely unexpected that this regression was missed. The likely path is that is that this module was failing consistently or very flaky before for another reason, so was marked skipped, which has masked this new error.

This is a general issue with CITGM right now. Last time I crunched the numbers, I realised of the 115 modules we had in the lookup at the time, at least 85 were marked as skipped or flaky on at least one platform or version. Both skip and flaky will mask errors. CITGM failures per run are ranging from 65-120 recently, which includes a lot of noise for the releaser to sift through to try and identify any new regressions. All of this unfortunately means we're less likely to catch regressions.

Releasers and various other contributors have worked to keep on top of the CITGM failures/flakes to keep the regression tool working as effectively as possible, but it's a never-ending challenge with too few people. Our team at Red Hat even had a dedicated 'CITGM greenness day' to try and resolve some failures and reduce noise but it was soon back up to where it is now. To resolve this I think we either need to be encouraging more contributions to keeping CITGM healthy, or explore alternative approaches.

For `package.json` it makes less sense - it's in a performance sensitive path, all the fields are optional, we generally only parse each file once, or lazy parse as much as possible (for imports/exports), and the happy path assumes all fields if present are valid - adding a round of eager schema validation would defeat the optimizations or introduce regressions e.g. when the fields are invalid, most of them have always been silently ignored.

I think regarding DoS, the use of a particular library underneath along doesn't provide strong enough guarantees, the implementation above can still have bugs that introduce e.g. complexity issues (e.g. for validators that handles untrusted input, an edge case that triggers a very long loop or a crash is a vulnerability, instead of just a regular bug). Generally it can be somewhat assured by more complete tests e.g. for boundaries, adversarial data sets e.g. https://github.com/nst/JSONTestSuite and many others, with fuzzing, etc. though none of it would really guarantee "there is absolutely no bug in this library" (as with any library). The best proof for how well something handles intentionally hostile input tends to be more battle testing and having it scrutinized by security researches who try to find and exploit edge cases in it.

Note that this would be a different requirement from regular JSON parsing in Node.js e.g. we do not guarantee DoS resistance in `JSON.parse()`, and parsing on known JSON files like `package.json` assume the input is trusted, so DoS does not apply. If implemented well a new JSON schema validator can help address the lack of a good DoS resistant validator in the wild, but if not it can be a new attack vector (for taking on responsibility that Node.js fails to guarantee).

fyi, i'm not really against or for this virtual fs (but it's going to sound like i'm against it - or maybe i'm slightly against it). 

But i just want  to raise something that hasn't been addressed in this discussion: I don't think the benefits here justify what this adds to Node.js core.

The reaction to this PR itself is a signal worth paying attention to: roughly **33% downvotes** on a Node.js core feature PR is unusually high. For most uncontroversial additions the opposition is in the low single digits. That level of disagreement from the community suggests the concerns here aren't just noise.

### The use cases already have solutions

**For testing/mocking:** A temporary directory in `os.tmpdir()` with cleanup afterwards is good enough for most cases. It's boring, it works everywhere, zero new APIs to learn.

**For in-memory use cases:** `Blob` and `File` already exist and cover the simple cases well. They're standardized and work in every runtime.

**For anything more serious:** Every major OS has built-in support for mounting virtual and RAM-backed filesystems. You get a real directory that every process sees — native addons, child processes, file descriptors, the permission model, everything just works. Zero lines added to Node.js core.

**For SEA assets specifically:** yes, an in-process solution makes sense here since there's no real path to mount. That's the one genuinely novel use case. But that's a much smaller, more focused feature than what this PR is.

### The cost to core is too high

* **21,645 lines** added to Node.js core
* **164+ manual interception hooks** in `lib/fs.js` and `lib/internal/fs/promises.js` that every future `fs` API addition must remember to include
* The bugs catalogued in this very issue exist because that surface area is nearly impossible to keep complete and correct — it will never be fully done
* Native addons and child processes still bypass VFS entirely, so it doesn't even fully solve the problem it sets out to solve

### The fragmentation problem

This is my bigger concern. If Node.js ships its own in-process VFS, Bun and Deno will either ignore it or ship their own incompatible version. We end up with yet another Node-specific API that library authors have to either avoid or special-case per runtime.

We already have this problem all over the place. Every time Node.js invents a non-web-standard API instead of aligning with or pushing for a web standard, it makes cross-runtime code harder. `Blob`, `File`, `ReadableStream`, OPFS — these exist so that code dealing with files and data doesn't have to care what runtime it's on. A `node:vfs` module goes in exactly the opposite direction.

I understand OPFS was considered and rejected — but the answer to "OPFS doesn't fit our needs" should be "let's work with the standards bodies to extend it", not "let's build our own thing in core."

### What I'd suggest instead

* If ppl need fast / non disk IO, then FUSE or ram disk might be the solution instead.
* Drop the general-purpose in-process VFS from core
* embrace OPFS & filesystem access that can make things work the same way across NodeJS and Browsers

The Node.js ecosystem is already massive. Adding permanent, hard-to-remove APIs to core should clear a much higher bar than this currently does.

Bugs exist in every subsystem. I wouldn't even consider these to be bugs at all. It's a work in progress and these are outstanding todos. 

> Native addons and child processes still bypass VFS entirely

And that's fine. Native addons have always been special and can bypass pretty much everything. If someone needed to, they could use the permission system to disable native addons.

> If Node.js ships its own in-process VFS, Bun and Deno will either ignore it or ship their own incompatible version

Or they'll duplicate it as part of their respective Node.js compatibility efforts (which is likely what we would do in cloudflare workers... at least to the extent there is overlap -- we don't have SEA or the same kind of module loader hooks). What other runtimes may or may not do relative to Node.js specific APIs really isn't much of a concern for us here. If this were implementing to a standard spec that would be a different matter.

## Worker threads don't inherit VFS mounts (SEA use case)

While integrating `@platformatic/vfs` (the userland polyfill of this PR) as the VFS layer for [@yao-pkg/pkg](https://github.com/yao-pkg/pkg) SEA mode, we discovered that **worker threads don't inherit VFS hooks from the main thread**. This affects real-world applications that use libraries like `pino` (via `thread-stream`), which spawn workers to handle log transport.

### The problem

When a SEA binary sets up VFS in the main thread and then a library spawns a `Worker` with a path inside the VFS mount (e.g., `/snapshot/node_modules/thread-stream/lib/worker.js`), the worker fails with:

```
Error: Cannot find module '/snapshot/node_modules/thread-stream/lib/worker.js'
```

This happens because:
1. VFS hooks (both `setVfsHandlers` at the C++ level and `Module.registerHooks` at the JS level) are per-Environment (per-isolate)
2. Worker threads get a fresh Environment with no VFS mounted
3. `node:sea` assets ARE process-wide (accessible from any thread), but nothing re-initializes the VFS in the worker

### Current workaround

We had to monkey-patch the `Worker` constructor to intercept `/snapshot/...` paths. For each intercepted worker:
1. Read the worker file from VFS in the main thread
2. Prepend a bundled VFS bootstrap (same `@platformatic/vfs` code, bundled separately by esbuild)
3. Pass the combined code via `new Worker(code, { eval: true })`

This works but is fragile — it requires bundling a separate copy of the VFS module hooks for workers, and `eval: true` has limitations (no real file URL, `import()` complications).

### Suggestion for `node:vfs`

Since `node:sea` assets are process-wide, the SEA VFS initialization (`lib/internal/vfs/sea.js`) could be extended to automatically run in worker threads too. Something like:

1. During SEA preparation, store the VFS config (mount point, provider type) in the SEA blob metadata
2. In `prepareWorkerThreadExecution` (or equivalent), check if running as SEA with VFS enabled
3. If so, call `initSeaVfs()` with the stored config to set up the same VFS mount in the worker

This would make SEA + VFS + worker threads work transparently without any userland patching.

Alternatively, a more general mechanism could allow VFS mounts to be "inherited" by workers, perhaps via a flag on the `Worker` constructor:

```js
new Worker('./worker.js', { inheritVFS: true })
```

### Context

- The test `test-vfs-chdir-worker.js` in this PR explicitly asserts that VFS is NOT shared with workers — so this is by-design, not a bug
- But for SEA use cases, this makes worker threads essentially broken unless the consumer implements the workaround above
- Libraries like pino, workerpool, jest-worker, and many others use worker threads
- The traditional `pkg` approach (C++ libuv-level patching) didn't have this issue since the patches were process-wide

Related: [yao-pkg/pkg#229](https://github.com/yao-pkg/pkg/pull/229), [platformatic/vfs#9](https://github.com/platformatic/vfs/pull/9), [platformatic/vfs#10](https://github.com/platformatic/vfs/pull/10)

## Root cause

This is a 32-bit integer overflow in `EncodeInto` in 
`src/encoding_binding.cc`:

\`\`\`cpp
size_t dest_length = dest->ByteLength();   // size_t — 2,390,753,275 OK

int nchars;
int written = source->WriteUtf8(
    isolate,
    write_result,
    dest_length,                            // implicit narrowing to int
    &nchars,
    String::NO_NULL_TERMINATION | String::REPLACE_INVALID_UTF8);
\`\`\`

`v8::String::WriteUtf8` takes the capacity as an `int`. When 
`dest_length` exceeds `INT32_MAX` (2,147,483,647), the narrowing 
conversion underflows to a negative number, V8 treats it as "no 
capacity", and writes 0 bytes — hence `{ read: 0, written: 0 }`.

The `subarray(offset, offset+10)` case works because the view is 
only 10 bytes, well within int range.

## Already fixed on main / v24

This was incidentally fixed by #58070 (`src: use non-deprecated 
WriteUtf8V2() method`), which migrated to `WriteUtf8V2` whose 
capacity parameter is `size_t`. The intent of that PR was 
deprecation cleanup, not bug fixing, but it resolved this issue as 
a side effect.

- v24.0.0+: fixed ✅
- v22.x: still affected ❌ (`int` capacity still in place)

## v22 LTS backport?

v22 is in maintenance LTS until 2027-04 and this causes silent data 
loss (not an error) for users with >2GB buffers. Would a minimal 
backport patch be acceptable — clamping the capacity to `INT_MAX` 
in `EncodeInto` specifically, rather than backporting the full 
WriteUtf8V2 migration?

## Additional Independent Verification: Minimal Reproduction with Detached Process (~4-6 seconds)

We independently encountered and diagnosed this exact issue while debugging a **Chrome Native Messaging host chain** for a browser automation tool. Our findings strongly corroborate the original report and provide a significantly tighter minimal reproduction window.

### Environment
- **Node.js**: v24.13.1 (crashes) vs v22.22.2 LTS (works)
- **OS**: Windows 11
- **Context**: Detached child processes spawned via `child_process.spawn` from within a Chrome Native Messaging host (`native-host.cjs`)

---

### Key Finding: Crash in 4-6 Seconds, Not 25 Minutes

Unlike the original report where the crash occurred after ~25 minutes of complex I/O (SSH, SFTP, tar), we isolated the issue to occur within **4-6 seconds** using a completely bare script with **zero I/O, zero external modules, and zero business logic**.

---

### Minimal Reproduction

**`worker.js`** — bare event loop, nothing else:
```javascript
// No I/O, no GC calls, no external modules, no business logic
setInterval(() => {}, 1000);
```

**`host.js`** — spawns worker as a detached process:
```javascript
const { spawn } = require('child_process');
const child = spawn(process.execPath, ['worker.js'], {
    detached: true,
    stdio: 'ignore',
    windowsHide: true
});
child.unref();
```

**Result on v24.13.1**: `worker.js` silently terminates via `TerminateProcess()` after ~4-6 seconds.  
**Result on v22.22.2**: `worker.js` survives indefinitely (tested 137+ seconds, manually stopped).

---

### Observations

1. **No Exit Handlers Fire**: We attached all available handlers — none triggered before the process vanished:
   ```javascript
   process.on('exit', () => log('exit'));
   process.on('SIGTERM', () => log('SIGTERM'));
   process.on('uncaughtException', () => log('uncaughtException'));
   // None of these print. The process simply disappears.
   ```

2. **Wrapper Independence**: Wrapping the spawn in `cmd.exe /c start` or `powershell.exe` did not prevent termination. Renaming `node.exe` to a custom binary name also had no effect.

3. **Digital Signature Verified**: `node.exe` has a valid digital signature (OpenJS Foundation, Microsoft-verified), ruling out AV/trust policy as the cause.

4. **Python Baseline**: An equivalent Python `time.sleep()` loop spawned as a detached process survives indefinitely under identical conditions, confirming this is Node.js-specific.

5. **Version-Specific**:
   | Node.js Version | Detached Process Lifetime |
   |---|---|
   | v24.13.1 | ~4-6 seconds ❌ |
   | v22.22.2 LTS | 137+ seconds ✅ |

---

### Impact in Our Use Case

This single bug explained **all** observed symptoms across 29 prior diagnostic tasks:
- Broker process "churn" every ~6-7 seconds
- `EPIPE` errors when the plugin wrote to a dead broker pipe
- Request timeouts for long-running browser tool calls
- Missing `process.on('exit')` traces (handlers never fired because `TerminateProcess()` bypasses JS cleanup)

What appeared to be a complex multi-layer failure in the Chrome extension ↔ native-host ↔ broker ↔ named-pipe chain was entirely caused by this single runtime regression.

---

### Workaround (Verified)

Downloading `node.exe` from the **v22.22.2 LTS** release and using it specifically to spawn the broker process resolved the issue completely:

```javascript
// native-host.cjs — use v22 binary for broker spawn
const nodeV22Path = path.join(path.dirname(BROKER_PATH), 'node-v22.exe');
const brokerNodeExe = fs.existsSync(nodeV22Path) ? nodeV22Path : process.execPath;

spawn(brokerNodeExe, [BROKER_PATH], {
    detached: true,
    stdio: 'ignore',
    windowsHide: true
});
```

After this change, the broker process (running on v22.22.2) survived **137+ seconds** with no crashes, and all browser automation tools (`browser_get_tabs`, `browser_navigate`, `browser_snapshot`) worked correctly.

---

Hope this additional data point — especially the minimal reproduction with a bare `setInterval` — helps narrow down the root cause in the runtime layer.

## Update: Windows Security Behavioral Detection Confirmed as Contributing Factor

After further investigation, we now have **direct evidence** that Windows Security (Defender) behavioral detection is killing detached child processes on Windows. This may be a contributing factor alongside any Node.js v24 runtime behavior.

### Evidence

On 2026-04-06 at 08:23 local time, while running minimal detached spawn reproduction tests with Node.js v24.13.1 on Windows 11, Windows Security flagged and terminated the test script:

- **Detection**: `Trojan:Win32/SuspExec.SE` (Suspicious Execution)
- **Status**: Removed (process killed)
- **Action**: The process was terminated immediately with no notification to the Node.js runtime

The Windows Security Protection History shows the exact command line that was flagged. The test script was a minimal reproduction: spawn a detached `node -e 'setInterval(()=>{},1000)'` child, then poll it with `process.kill(pid, 0)`.

### Why This Pattern Triggers Detection

Windows Security behavioral analysis flags this pattern because it resembles C2 beacon/persistence behavior:

1. PowerShell writes a script to disk
2. Script spawns a detached, never-exiting child process
3. Parent polls child liveness at regular intervals
4. Child has no visible I/O or user-facing activity

This is indistinguishable from malware persistence techniques at the behavioral level.

### Key Observation: Other Tools Work Fine

On the same machine, other browser automation tools work without issues:
- **Claude Code** (desktop): browser automation works perfectly
- **Manus AI** (web): browser automation works perfectly

This suggests the issue is not purely a Node.js v24 runtime bug. If it were, all Node.js-based tools would be equally affected.

### Revised Hypothesis

The root cause is likely a **combination of factors**:

1. **Windows Security behavioral detection** (confirmed): kills processes that match the SuspExec pattern, regardless of digital signature validity. The detection is behavior-based, not signature-based.
2. **Node.js v24 compatibility**: Windows Security may not have whitelisted/recognized the behavioral profile of Node.js v24 yet (newer runtime = fewer established behavioral patterns = higher false positive rate).
3. **Spawn pattern similarity to malware**: `detached: true + stdio: 'ignore' + child.unref()` + polling is exactly how many persistence implants work.

### Why Node v22 LTS Works

Node v22 LTS has been around longer. Windows Security has likely built behavioral whitelisting for common Node.js v22 spawn patterns. Node v24 is newer and its behavioral profile may not be fully recognized yet.

### Updated Workaround

In addition to using Node v22 LTS, also consider:

1. Add your project directory to **Windows Security exclusions** (Settings > Privacy & Security > Windows Security > Virus & Threat Protection > Exclusions)
2. Use Node v22 LTS for spawning long-lived detached processes: `nvm install 22 && nvm use 22`
3. If developing/testing detached spawn patterns on Windows, be aware that Windows Security real-time protection may silently kill your processes

This finding also explains the "invisible hand" effect we observed: processes dying after ~4-6 seconds with zero diagnostic output, zero JS exit handlers firing, and zero Event Log entries. Windows Security `TerminateProcess()` produces exactly this symptom profile.

## ⚠️ Correction: Root Cause Was Windows Defender, Not Node v24 Bug

**TL;DR:** Our original diagnosis was wrong. The actual root cause was **Windows Defender behavior detection** (`Trojan:Win32/SuspExec.SE`), not Node.js v24 silently terminating detached processes.

### What Changed

After adding Windows Defender exclusions for `OpenCode.exe`, `opencode-cli.exe`, `node.exe`, and their install directories:

- **Node v24.13.1 detached spawn**: ✅ Stable 8+ seconds (previously died at 4-6s)
- **Chrome headless launch**: ✅ Normal (previously killed by Defender)
- **CDP browser automation (full chain)**: ✅ Tab create → navigate → JS eval → DOM modify → close — all pass

The same Node v24.13.1 binary, same code, same machine — the only change was Defender exclusions.

### Corrected Diagnosis

| Before (Wrong) | After (Correct) |
|----------------|-----------------|
| Node v24 silently terminates detached children via `TerminateProcess()` | Windows Defender behavior detection flags AI coding agent processes as `Trojan:Win32/SuspExec.SE` and kills them |
| Workaround: downgrade to Node v22 | Workaround: add Defender exclusions for AI coding tools |
| nodejs/node#62125 is the root cause | nodejs/node#62125 may still be a real issue under other conditions, but **our specific reproduction case was Defender** |

### Why the Misdiagnosis

1. `TerminateProcess()` was called — but by Windows Defender, not Node.js internals
2. No exit handlers fired — because Defender's `TerminateProcess()` is a forced kill, identical behavior to what we attributed to Node
3. Python survived — not because of language differences, but because Defender's heuristic didn't flag Python processes the same way
4. Digital signature was valid — Defender uses behavioral heuristics, not just signature checks

### Evidence Log

- Windows Security popup: `Trojan:Win32/SuspExec.SE` detected during debugging session
- Claude Code and Manus AI browser automation worked fine on same machine (different process signatures)
- After Defender exclusions: all tests pass, including bare `setInterval` detached spawn on v24.13.1

**Apologies for the initial misattribution.** The nodejs/node#62125 issue may still be valid for other reporters — we can only correct our own reproduction case.

When I added my thoughts to this almost 3 years ago there was confusion as to what the standard is.  The protocol standard is [RFC6455](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6455) while the browser API specification is [WHATWG WebSocket Interface](https://websockets.spec.whatwg.org/#the-websocket-interface).  People were more concerned with the later while ignoring the former, which I found problematic because Node is not a web browser, regardless the former is needed in any context.

In the browser the new [WebTransport](https://www.w3.org/TR/webtransport/) recommendation is expected to largely replace WebSockets, but only in the browser.  WebTransport requires use of the HTTPS scheme, requires use of TLS, and is based upon [HTTP/3](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/HTTP/3).  In the browser that is fine, because from a transmission context the browser is an extremely limited single use interface with its own unique constraints.  Outside the browser using UDP to mimic TCP connections for mild performance boosts is a really bad idea because you lose the benefits of both UDP and TCP.  TCP is single-cast only because it is connection oriented.  Since UDP is connection-less, doesn't care about message integrity, it can support multicast transmissions, which is why it has a wildly different encryption scheme when used outside the browser: [DTLS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Datagram_Transport_Layer_Security).  Also, a WebSocket service does not require HTTP of any version in any way, and can listen on the same port as a HTTP server without conflict.

In the mean time if you want WebSockets for Node that are close to the metal, as close as allowed using a Node only approach, you can look to these poorly examples:

* connection - https://github.com/prettydiff/aphorio/blob/main/lib/transmit/connection.ts#L249-L262
* message send - https://github.com/prettydiff/aphorio/blob/main/lib/transmit/send.ts
* message receive - https://github.com/prettydiff/aphorio/blob/main/lib/transmit/receiver.ts

I believe the root cause here is a V8 change, not `abort_controller.js`.

V8 commit [`5abdd62d579b`](https://chromium.googlesource.com/v8/v8/+/5abdd62d579b7f6e1403dc1c41619f736d7cdc62) ("Don't pretenure WeakCells", Sep 2025) changed how `FinalizationRegistry` allocates its internal `WeakCell` objects. Before that commit, WeakCells went directly to old space (`Pretenured`). Now they land in young generation, where they're treated as strong roots during minor GCs (tracked in [chromium:340777103](https://issues.chromium.org/issues/340777103)).

`AbortSignal.any()` calls `FinalizationRegistry.register()` on every invocation. In patterns like request handlers with a shared controller, WeakCell entries pile up in young space faster than minor GC can clear them. Major GC does collect them, but it doesn't run often enough at high call rates.

I restored the `Pretenured` flag on V8 14.3 and rebuilt Node to confirm. The leak goes away - memory stays flat at ~162 MiB instead of growing past 2 GB.

This looks like a regression introduced by #52050, which moved `mode` validation from JS (`parseFileMode`) to the C++ layer.

The value `2176057344` is within the UInt32 range but exceeds the Int32 range, so the C++ assertion `args[2]->IsInt32()` in `src/node_file.cc` crashes instead of throwing a catchable `RangeError`.

I'd like to work on a fix. I see two possible approaches:

**Approach A**: Change `parseFileMode()` in `lib/internal/validators.js` to use `validateInt32` instead of `validateUint32`, aligning JS validation with the C++ expectation. This is cleaner but affects all `fs` functions that use `parseFileMode` and could be considered semver-major.

**Approach B**: Keep `parseFileMode()` as-is, and only add `parseFileMode()` calls in the `ReadStream`/`WriteStream` constructors in `lib/internal/fs/streams.js` with an additional Int32 range check. This minimizes the impact but is less consistent.

Which approach would be preferred? I'll also add regression tests for both `createWriteStream` and `createReadStream` with this value.

Title: ESM loader: infinite recursion stack overflow on malformed cyclic exports instead of clear error

  Summary

  When a large single-file bundled ESM package has corrupted cyclic re-exports due to installation corruption, Node.js 22+ ESM
  loader will go into infinite recursion until stack overflow, instead of throwing a clear error message about cyclic
  dependency or reaching max recursion depth.

  Steps to reproduce

  1. npm install -g openclaw — installation somehow gets corrupted (likely network interrupt during unpacking)，resulting in
  extra cyclic re-exports in the bundled file
  2. Try to run openclaw gateway start
  3. It crashes with RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded in compileSourceTextModule inside Node.js ESM loader

  Expected behavior

  - Should detect cyclic dependency or max recursion depth
  - Throw a clear error like "Too many recursive dependency resolutions detected" instead of silent stack overflow
  - It shouldn't infinite recursion no matter how bad the module is

  Actual behavior

  - Infinite recursion until stack overflow, no clear error message
  - You have to guess what's wrong from the stack overflow

  Affected versions

  - Node.js 22.x — confirmed
  - Probably affects 23.x/24.x/25+ too since the loader code is the same
  - Node.js 20.x doesn't have this issue — it seems the different loading order accidentally tolerates this corrupted case

  Workaround

  - npm install -g openclaw --force reinstall fixes the corrupted package
  - After reinstall, even default stack size works fine

  Suggestions for improvement

  1. Add a maximum recursion depth check in ESM module loading
  2. When max depth is reached, throw a clear error instead of continuing to infinite recursion
  3. This improves robustness when dealing with corrupted or malformed bundled modules

Update: I found an existing issue that appears to be the same root cause:
https://github.com/nodejs/node/issues/52864

That issue demonstrates the stack overflow with a minimal circular ESM import.
My case is a more complex manifestation: a large bundled file with many 
cyclic re-exports (common in CLI tools built with esbuild/rollup).

This suggests the underlying problem is the ESM loader's handling of 
circular dependencies in Node.js 22+, which manifests both in:
- Simple two-file cycles (#52864)
- Large bundled files with cyclic re-exports (this issue)

I see three possibilities:

1. Have only `partialDeepStrictEqual()` (current version)
   - Advantage: We know that `partialDeepStrictEqual()` does not exist in legacy mode.
   - Disadvantage: In strict mode, all methods have aliases without `strict` except `partialDeepStrictEqual()`.
2. Have `partialDeepStrictEqual()` and `partialDeepEqual()` (the worst-case scenario 👎)
   - Advantage: All methods exist in both modes, and they are all aliases without _strict_ in strict mode.
   - Disadvantage: You have to add a deprecated method.
3. Have `partialDeepStrictEqual()` and its alias `partialDeepEqual()` only in strict mode (my suggestion ❤️)
   - Advantage: All methods have their aliases without `strict` in strict mode.
   - Disadvantage: `partialDeepEqual()` only exists in strict mode.

---

In my projects, I only use strict mode and aliases without `strict`. Aliases allow for shorter method names and make the code more readable. I'd really like to have the `partialDeepEqual()` alias (only in strict mode) for these two reasons, as well as to maintain consistency in my asserts.

The shape of the `assert` and `assert/strict` modules should remain equivalent. We shouldn't start adding pseudo-aliases to one that don't exist in the other, particularly when the only real argument is "it looks nicer".

Having `strict` in any of our names is not ideal and it is purely a legacy issue that we can not really solve.

The strict mode was implemented with avoiding that word while still having the overall implementation as expected. I slightly lean on the third suggestion therefore (adding the alias in strict mode only), while I also very well understand the reasoning of @Renegade334 to not introduce a pseudo-alias. This is a tricky not perfect API world and either way it is not ideal.
I’d prefer 2; i weigh consistency more highly than “non-strict methods are icky”

Your student is partially correct.

URLs are a subset of URIs. That is, all URLs are URIs. So it is true to say that all http request URL's are actually URIs.

But, if we look at the RFC: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7230.html#section-5.3 ... you'll find that the `/pub/WWW` part of `GET /pub/WWW/ HTTP/1.1` is not actually always a URI... it is *derived* from the target URI.

That part of the request line is called the `request-target`, which has this definition:

```
Once an inbound connection is obtained, the client sends an HTTP
request message ([Section 3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7230.html#section-3)) with a request-target derived from the
target URI.  There are four distinct formats for the request-target,
depending on both the method being requested and whether the request
is to a proxy.

     request-target = origin-form
                    / absolute-form
                    / authority-form
                    / asterisk-form
```

The `origin-form` is an `absolute-path` plus an optional query. The `absolute-path` is nothing more than a sequence of one or more `/`-delimited `segments`. This would make it a `path-absolute` in URI terms (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3986#section-3.3) or possibly a `path-noscheme`, and not an actual URI.

Only the `absolute-form` option is an `absolute-URI`. The rest aren't.

That all said, most developers are way more familiar with the term `url` than they are with the term `uri`, and most http applications use `url` rather than `uri` in commmon practice. So in this case, the API was named for the most common expectation rather than the most correct terminology.

We’ve run into the same pattern in a real long-running production workload (Lodestar beacon-node req/resp networking).

In our case, each req/resp round-trip composed a request abort signal with a response-timeout signal. Over time, those composed signals accumulated in the networking worker and showed up as steady old-space growth in heap snapshots.

The important part is that this was **not** a tight same-tick synthetic loop — it was normal long-lived request/response traffic on a running node.

Our mitigation on the application side was to stop using `AbortSignal.any(...)` for that path and instead manually compose the signals with explicit listener cleanup once the response stream closes. That change is here:
- https://github.com/ChainSafe/lodestar/pull/9029

So from our side, this issue is not just microbenchmark-only — we hit the same retention shape in a real networking path.

Conclusion: In v8.11.4, the read side was unexpectedly opened as well, allowing the entire socket lifecycle to be driven to completion by read-side events (EOF/HUP). Calling read(0) on the write side is somewhat unusual and unnecessary. TL;DR createSocket() first executes new net.Socket({ handle: pipe }). Because options.readable is not explicitly passed, the net.Socket constructor assumes the socket is readable and calls read(0). read(0) triggers _read(), which in turn calls the underlying _handle.readStart(), causing libuv to start listening for read events on this handle. Later, createSocket() sets s.readable = false (semantically making stdin "write-only"). However, the steps above have already occurred—the read loop has already been started. Then, when the child process executes fs.closeSync(0): It closes the stdin file descriptor on the child process's side. For the underlying file descriptor on the parent process's side, the kernel may generate a "closed on the other end" readable-side event (EOF/HUP, etc., depending on the details of the pipe/socketpair). After the event loop receives the EOF/HUP event, the following calls are triggered: endWritableNT is called within endReadableNT. Finally, the entire socket is destroyed and the close event is triggered: ```text endReadableNT endWritableNT NET 97229: _final: not ended, call shutdown() NET 97229: afterShutdown destroyed=false NET 97229: destroy NET 97229: close NET 97229: close handle NET 97229: emit close ``` This is why cp.stdin.on('close') was triggered. But after v8.11.4, read(0) will no longer be called. As a result, the event loop will not receive EOF/HUP events, nor will it trigger calls to endWritableNT and endReadableNT. Consequently, cp.stdin.on('close') will no longer be triggered.

I have an idea, but I'm not sure if it's feasible: add two methods to pipe_wrap.cc.

- `WatchPeerClose`, in the method call the `uv_read_start` method to inject a listener for the EOF/HUP event. Once the event is detected, a JS callback is triggered to execute, which in turn triggers a method to destroy the socket.

- `UnWatchPeerClose`, in the method call the `uv_read_stop` method to unregister the listener.

From what I can tell, this seems consistent with current Node.js behavior rather than an OpenSSL-side bug.

Node loads OpenSSL configuration during startup, and in this case the configuration load failure appears to be treated as fatal:
https://github.com/nodejs/node/blob/8ccbe8e38430d278455ac2ed3a5e2aa4c7acfcce/src/node.cc#L1176-L1187

The CLI docs also describe startup loading of the default OpenSSL configuration file (`openssl.cnf`), which can be changed via `OPENSSL_CONF` or `--openssl-config`, but they do not provide a startup option to skip config loading entirely:
https://nodejs.org/api/cli.html#openssl-shared-config

If different behavior is desired, that would likely be a Node.js behavior change request rather than an OpenSSL bug.

I've been making very good progress on this recently: with #62217 and #62254, it will be possible to sufficiently control the fingerprint of a Node TLS connection to exactly match the JA4 fingerprints for Chrome, Firefox or curl (and basically anything else AFAIK - those are just my goto test cases).

JA3 has been obsoleted by Chrome's random extension ordering & GREASE work, but we will eventually get relatively close to that anyway - with the next OpenSSL bump (Node v27 I think) we'll get my fixes for https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/26990 EC point formats which is the main outstanding gap there. All the changes here will generally make Node's TLS less distinctive, so even the default fingerprint will be much closer to standard practices everywhere else.

Full fingerprint control won't be available directly within Node itself (there's plenty of weirdness & footguns here, supporting this as a built-in isn't a good idea) but it'd be easy to implement from a native addon that could integrate into the normal Node TLS APIs - so you can use standard TLS/HTTPS APIs or anything that depends on them, but control the fingerprint at the same time.

Once the above PRs are merged & released, I'll publish a package using them to do this, and then finally we can close this issue (after just 5 short years...). If anybody wants to review those to help find & finish up any issues there that'd be very welcome.

I don't understand. You can already write new code that is incompatible between browsers and node.js by using the returned Timeout object. I see plenty of new code use .unref() or .refresh().

I think the concern is more about creating *more* of a discrepancy and introducing an additional, more obscure error condition. If we take the "It's a node.js timeout so it doesn't matter" point of view then we likely are doing a disservice for cross-runtime interop/portability.

Would it be feasible on the ~~very~~ long term to have separate timers implementations? I.e. `globalThis.setTimeout()` that tries its best to follow the HTML spec, and `node:timers.setTimeout()`&`node:timers/promises.setTimeout()` that are not bound by interoperability constraints anymore.

I think we should just create new Node.js timer APIs that do all the things we want (return objects, disposable) and then we aren't tied to browser spec. We should support setTimeout and setImmediate as standardized, and then have separate APIs (call them delay or sleep or whatever else) and then it's the users choice if they need interop code to use the browser ones, and if not use the node ones.

Sadly, while I agree in concept, I suspect that deprecating our current setTimeout/setInterval return values would be quite difficult... On par with the deprecation of the Buffer constructor. I don't know if we'd be able to get there.

Any existing userland code that uses Node.js is using the `node:timers` implementation. How about this:
1. Deprecate accessing `setTimeout`/`setInterval`/ etc. as globals in favour of explicitly importing them from `node:timers`.
2. Keep the implementation independent from the HTML spec.
3. After EOL, reintroduce `globalThis.setTimeout` with behavior as close to the browser version as possible.

For users relying on Node.js's implementation, adding explicit `import`/`require` (which already should be a recommended practice) would be sufficient. They will retain full functionality with promises, disposers, refresh, etc.
For users using `globalThis.setTimeout` in browser-compatible way, nothing would change and they may get even more compatibility (such as implicit eval...).

IMHO this is much better than being stuck forever with an API that is both incompatible and unable to evolve.

I think we are steering away from the topic - if there are no plans of deprecating or changing the return type, then I don't really see the justification for removing Symbol.dispose from Timeout.

Secondly, I agree they can/should be removed in order to best facilitate interoperability across the ecosystem.
